questions.prompt: What makes a function type useful?
options: It replaces all runtime error handling.
It documents parameter and return contracts so callers and implementations can be checked consistently.
It automatically tests the function at runtime.
It causes the function to run when the type is declared.
questions.answer_key: It documents parameter and return contracts so callers and implementations can be checked consistently.
questions.explanation: Function types are compile-time contracts and should be paired with behavior tests.

questions.prompt: Which statement is correct about “Generic Functions”?
options: The concept should be demonstrated with type parameters on functions and checked against its intended contract.
The safest approach is to skip diagnostics and trust the first output.
A type assertion automatically validates every value at runtime.
The learner should publish hidden solutions so the exercise can grade itself.
questions.answer_key: The concept should be demonstrated with type parameters on functions and checked against its intended contract.
questions.explanation: The supplied syllabus explicitly includes “Type parameters on functions”; connect it to a concrete example and verify the behavior relevant to this lesson.

questions.prompt: What is a good verification step after practicing “Generic Functions”?
options: Assume inferring generic type arguments is unnecessary because the code has type annotations.
Ignore compiler or test failures if the interface looks correct.
Treat passing a static token check as proof that the program executed correctly.
Check preserving input-to-output relationships, include a meaningful failure case where appropriate, and document any runtime or version assumptions.
questions.answer_key: Check preserving input-to-output relationships, include a meaningful failure case where appropriate, and document any runtime or version assumptions.
questions.explanation: The syllabus includes “Preserving input-to-output relationships”. Verification should match the concept: type-level checks, runtime tests, configuration checks or human review as appropriate.
